title: Graph data & why the naive approach fails

hook.title: The seating chart
hook.text: A dinner party can be described by a **seating chart**: who is next to whom, plus a note about each guest. Photos have a natural order (pixel row 1, row 2, …) and sentences too (word 1, word 2, …). A party does not: you can list the guests in *any* order and it is still the same party. Now imagine stapling the guest list and the 'who sits next to whom' table into one long vector and feeding it to a standard neural net. Re-list the guests alphabetically and the vector changes completely, though nothing about the party changed.
hook.recall: Remember the seating chart: the same party can be written down in $|V|!$ ways. A network that sees a different input for each way can’t learn the party itself.

explore.intro: One six-node graph. Press the button to list its nodes in a different order.
tasks: Re-order the nodes several times. Does the *graph picture* ever change? What changes in the adjacency table?
Compare the naive MLP output with the neighbour-averaging layer + sum readout.
explore.takeaway: Graphs have no canonical node ordering. A model on $[A\,|\,X]$ gives different outputs for relabelings of the same graph; a model built from neighbourhood aggregation does not.

build.prompt: Order the argument for why the naive approach fails (slides 7–8).
items: Join the adjacency matrix $A$ and the feature matrix $X$ into one input
Feed the result into an ordinary neural network
Re-label (permute) the nodes: this is the same graph
The input vector changes, so the network can output something different for the same graph
build.explanation: The graph does not have a canonical order of nodes, so the naive approach has different inputs for the same graph.

questions.prompt: Which property of graph data makes the naive “feed $A$ and $X$ to an MLP” approach fail?
options: Graphs have no canonical node ordering
questions.explanation: The seating chart can be written in many orders; an MLP treats each as a different input.

questions.prompt: A graph has $|V|=6$ nodes. How many different node-order plans exist ($|V|!$)?
Which statement about graph-structured data is FALSE?
options: Networks can have arbitrary size and complex topology
There is no fixed node ordering or reference point
Networks are often dynamic with multimodal features
Graphs come with a canonical node order like the pixels of an image
questions.explanation: Images and text have a natural order; graphs don’t.

questions.prompt: In the naive approach, what is the problem with using the same graph under two different node orderings?
options: Two different inputs for the same graph
questions.explanation: “The naive approach would have different inputs for the same graph.”

questions.prompt: *“The adjacency matrices under two node orderings look different, so they describe two different graphs, and the MLP is right to output different values.”* What’s wrong?
options: Both orderings are the *same graph* relabelled; a graph model should give the same graph-level output
The adjacency matrices are always equal

questions.prompt: Which data types have a natural fixed ordering (recap slide)?
questions.explanation: Pixels on a grid; words in a sequence. Networks don’t.
